tagline: Gold, cocoa, and the rhythm of highlife
overview:
Ghana lies on the Gulf of Guinea in West Africa, between Ivory Coast, Burkina Faso, and Togo, and is about the size of Oregon. Its capital, Accra, is a fast-growing coastal city of markets, beaches, and tech start-ups, and it is one of the closest big cities in the world to the point where the equator meets the prime meridian. The country's name was borrowed from a medieval African empire, and its old colonial name, the Gold Coast, told of the metal that drew traders for centuries.

About 34 million people live in Ghana, and English is the official language, though most people speak Akan languages such as Twi, or Ewe, Ga, or Dagbani at home. Ghana was the first country in sub-Saharan Africa to win independence from European colonial rule, in 1957, and today it is one of the continent's most stable democracies, a republic that has handed power peacefully between parties several times. Ghana is the world's second-largest producer of cocoa, a major gold miner, and famous across Africa for its music, colorful kente cloth, and friendly spirit.
landAndNature: Ghana is mostly low plains and plateaus. The south has a coastline of sandy beaches, lagoons, and old forts, backed by tropical forests where cocoa trees grow in the shade. The Akwapim-Togo hills run along the eastern border, with Mount Afadja, at 885 meters, the highest point. In the center lies Lake Volta, created by the Akosombo Dam in 1965 and one of the largest human-made lakes in the world by surface area. The north is dry savanna with baobabs and shea trees, where Mole National Park shelters elephants, antelope, and baboons. Kakum National Park has a rope walkway strung high in the rainforest canopy. Rain is heaviest in the southwest, and the harmattan wind brings dust from the Sahara in winter.
peopleAndCulture: The Akan, including the Ashanti, are the largest group, with the Ewe, Ga-Adangbe, Mole-Dagbani, and many others. Most Ghanaians are Christian, with a large Muslim community in the north. Kente cloth, woven in bright strips by Ashanti and Ewe weavers, is worn at ceremonies, and Adinkra symbols stamped on fabric carry proverbs. Fufu, pounded cassava and plantain, is dipped in light soup or groundnut soup, and jollof rice sparks a friendly rivalry with Nigeria. Highlife music, born here in the early 1900s, and modern hiplife and Afrobeats fill the airwaves. Soccer is a passion; the Black Stars have won the Africa Cup of Nations four times. Funerals are huge celebrations of life, sometimes with custom-built coffins shaped like fish, cars, or airplanes.
history: Trading kingdoms rose here by the 1000s, and from about 1700 the Ashanti Empire, ruled from Kumasi and symbolized by a sacred Golden Stool, grew rich and powerful. Portuguese traders built Elmina Castle in 1482, the oldest European building in sub-Saharan Africa, and over the following centuries dozens of forts along the coast held enslaved Africans before shipment across the Atlantic. Britain fought several wars with the Ashanti and made the Gold Coast a colony in the 1800s. Led by Kwame Nkrumah, Ghana became independent on March 6, 1957, inspiring independence movements across Africa. Nkrumah was overthrown in 1966, and coups followed until 1992, when a new constitution brought lasting multiparty democracy. Ghana became an oil producer in 2010.
funFacts: Ghana's Lake Volta is one of the largest reservoirs in the world, covering about 8,500 square kilometers.
The Ashanti Golden Stool is believed to hold the soul of the nation and is never allowed to touch the ground.
Ghanaian craftsmen build fantasy coffins shaped like lions, sneakers, cocoa pods, and cameras to honor the dead.
Ghana is the second-largest cocoa producer in the world, growing much of the chocolate eaten in Europe.
Elmina Castle, built in 1482, is the oldest European building still standing south of the Sahara.
